title: Area VIII review: High-Altitude Operations
intro: These questions mix the two Tasks of Area VIII, supplemental oxygen and pressurization. Many of them join both in one high flight, because a pressurization problem quickly becomes an oxygen problem.

questions.q: Part 91, pressurized single at 24,000 ft. A controller fault leaves the system holding only 2.9 psi differential, and terrain keeps you at 24,000 ft for 50 minutes. Using the chart shown, what does 91.211 require?
options: The required crew uses oxygen the whole 50 minutes, since the cabin is at 14,000 ft
Each occupant must be provided with oxygen, since the airplane is above 15,000 ft
The required crew uses oxygen for the last 20 minutes; the passengers need nothing
Nothing, because the cabin is still pressurized
questions.why: Cabin pressure is outside pressure plus the differential. The chart gives 5.7 psi at 24,000 ft, so 5.7 + 2.9 = 8.6 psi, which is the 14,000 ft row [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]. 91.211 counts cabin pressure altitude. Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft, the crew uses oxygen for the part of the flight over 30 minutes: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes. Passengers come in only above 15,000 ft cabin altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The 'whole 50 minutes' answer misses the words 'up to and including'; the whole-flight rule starts above 14,000 ft. The airplane's own altitude does not matter for paragraph (a).

questions.q: A pressurized airplane decompresses at FL 270 and you pull on your diluter-demand mask. The regulator has a Normal (automix) setting and a 100 percent setting. Which setting do you use?
options: 100 percent
Normal, because the automix gives the right mix for the cabin altitude
Normal at first, then 100 percent only if you feel symptoms
Off until the descent is set up, to save oxygen
questions.why: The PHAK recommends that crewmembers select the 100 percent setting on a demand or pressure-demand regulator at high altitude [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], and the AC's drill is mask on in 5 seconds or less, check for flow, breathe 100 percent oxygen [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Normal is tempting, but most regulators approved to 40,000 ft change to 100 percent oxygen only at about 34,000 ft cabin altitude [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], so below that the automix still blends in cabin air, and the cabin after this decompression is near 27,000 ft. Waiting for symptoms is wrong too: impaired performance may be immediate, and prompt use of 100 percent oxygen is critical [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

questions.q: At FL 240 a side window cracks with a bang and the cabin fills with white mist. A passenger shouts 'Fire!' What is the mist most likely to be, and what comes first?
options: Smoke from an electrical fire; use the extinguisher first
Oxygen escaping from the masks; turn off the oxygen first
Air conditioning condensation; no action is needed
Fog from the sudden drop in temperature and change in humidity; masks on first
questions.why: In an explosive decompression the cabin fills with fog, dust or debris, and the fog comes from the rapid drop in temperature and the change in relative humidity [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. The primary danger of a decompression is hypoxia, so quick use of the oxygen equipment comes first, then a rapid descent [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Reaching for the extinguisher first spends useful consciousness on the wrong problem, and calling the mist harmless leaves you without oxygen.

questions.q: Your pressurized single has no fixed oxygen installation, so a portable kit is your only oxygen on a flight to FL 250. You stow it in the aft baggage compartment, which you can reach only from outside on the ground. What is wrong with this?
options: It is missing the 10-minute descent supply that 91.211(b) requires at FL 250
The kit is out of reach: the PHAK and AC say portable oxygen must be readily accessible in flight, and after a rapid decompression at 25,000 ft you may have only about 90 seconds
Nothing, because you can descend below 12,500 ft before anyone needs oxygen
A portable kit may serve only the passengers, so the pilot needs a fixed system
questions.why: If an airplane has no fixed installation, portable oxygen equipment must be readily accessible during flight, says the PHAK [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and AC 61-107B says the same [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. That is guidance from those two sources, not a line in 91.211 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. AC Figure 2-3 gives 1.5 to 2.5 minutes of useful consciousness at 25,000 ft after a rapid decompression, and you plan with the lower value: 1.5 x 60 = 90 seconds [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. A bottle you cannot reach does not help. The 10-minute supply in 91.211(b) starts only above FL 250, so at FL 250 it is not the problem [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

questions.q: Your pressurized single decompresses rapidly at FL 250, and your emergency descent averages 3,000 fpm. If you dived first and put the mask on later, about how long until the cabin is below 12,500 ft, and what does that tell you?
options: About 4.2 minutes, which is inside the 3 to 5 minutes of useful consciousness, so diving first is fine
About 2.5 minutes, which is inside your useful consciousness, so diving first is fine
About 8.3 minutes, so you have time to troubleshoot first
About 4.2 minutes, which is longer than the 1.5 to 2.5 minutes you have after a rapid decompression, so the mask goes on first
questions.why: With no pressurization the cabin follows the airplane down: (25,000 - 12,500) / 3,000 = 4.2 minutes. AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 3 to 5 minutes at 25,000 ft, but only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes after a rapid decompression, and you assume the lower value [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. So 4.2 minutes is longer than your useful time, and the mask goes on first, in 5 seconds or less, then you descend [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The '3 to 5 minutes' choice reads the wrong column. 8.3 minutes is 25,000 / 3,000, the time to sea level, not to 12,500 ft.

questions.q: Part 91, pressurized single at 22,000 ft. A controller fault leaves the system holding only 2.2 psi differential, and you stay at 22,000 ft for 40 minutes. Using the chart shown and interpolating between the 14,000 and 16,000 ft rows, what does 91.211 require?
options: The required crew uses oxygen only for the part over 30 minutes, which is 10 minutes; passengers need nothing
The required crew uses oxygen the whole 40 minutes; passengers do not have to be provided with oxygen
The required crew uses oxygen the whole 40 minutes, and each passenger must be provided with oxygen
Nothing, because the cabin is still pressurized
questions.why: Cabin pressure is outside pressure plus the differential: 6.2 + 2.2 = 8.4 psi [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]. Between the 14,000 ft row (8.6 psi) and the 16,000 ft row (8.0 psi): 14,000 + (8.6 - 8.4) / (8.6 - 8.0) x 2,000 = 14,667 ft. Above 14,000 ft the required crew must use oxygen for the entire time at those altitudes, with no 30-minute allowance; every occupant must be provided with oxygen only above 15,000 ft cabin altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. At 22,000 ft the airplane is also below FL 250, so the 10-minute descent supply is not in play.

questions.q: Intense smoke fills the cabin of your pressurized single at FL 230. Four people are aboard, but there are oxygen masks only for the two front seats. What does the AFH point you toward?
options: An emergency descent, since depressurizing at altitude is an option only when oxygen is available for all occupants
Dumping the cabin pressure at altitude to clear the smoke, since two masks are enough
Staying pressurized and level, since the pressurization air will clear any smoke
Turning the oxygen to full flow so everyone can share it, and holding altitude
questions.why: On pressurized airplanes the pressurization air removes smoke, but if the smoke is intense it may be necessary to depressurize at altitude, if oxygen is available for all occupants, or to make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. With masks for only two of four, dumping the cabin at FL 230 would leave two people hypoxic, so the descent is the choice. 'Stay level and wait' fails because intense smoke is exactly the case where the AFH says action may be needed. Holding altitude on shared oxygen also ignores AC 61-107B, which says that because oxygen is so combustible, a fire at high altitude means an immediate descent to an altitude that does not require oxygen [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]].

questions.q: You plan FL 270 in a pressurized single. The oxygen for everyone aboard, pilot included, is a continuous-flow system. What does AC 61-107B say about it?
options: Continuous flow is approved only up to 18,000 ft, so you need masks
It is as safe as pressure demand at any altitude, so no extra attention is needed
It is certificated up to 41,000 ft but needs very careful attention above 25,000 ft, and pilots should use the masks meant for them
It must be replaced by a pressure-demand system above 25,000 ft
questions.why: AC 61-107B says continuous-flow systems are certificated up to 41,000 ft MSL, but their capabilities need very careful attention above 25,000 ft MSL. Pilot masks sometimes allow more flow than passenger masks, so pilots should use the masks meant for them [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. The 18,000 ft figure is the PHAK's masks-instead-of-cannulas line, not a limit on continuous flow [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. Pressure demand is the system the PHAK calls safe above 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]], but nothing requires a swap at 25,000 ft.

questions.q: After a decompression at FL 250 and your descent, a passenger has a deep ache in her knee that gets worse when she moves it. She wants to stretch it out. What do you do?
options: Let her stretch it; joint pain after a flight is usually a cramp from sitting
Keep the knee still, keep her on 100 percent oxygen, land as soon as possible and get her evaluated
Continue to the destination, since bends pain always goes away once you are below 10,000 ft
Take her mask off now that you are low, and have her walk the cabin to work the pain out
questions.why: Deep joint pain that gets worse when the joint moves is the bends, the most common sign of altitude decompression sickness [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]] [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. The PHAK steps are: mask on at 100 percent, descend and land as soon as possible, keep a painful joint still and do not try to work the pain out, and get medical help after landing [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Bends pain can start at altitude, during the descent or many hours later [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]], so 'it goes away below 10,000 ft' is not a safe bet.

questions.q: You fly a Part 135 charter in a pressurized single at FL 230 with the cabin at 8,000 ft. Must the passenger briefing before takeoff cover the normal and emergency use of oxygen?
options: No, because 135.117 follows cabin pressure altitude and the cabin is only 8,000 ft
No, because oxygen is briefed only in unpressurized airplanes
Yes, but only if the flight spends more than 30 minutes above 12,000 ft MSL
Yes, because the flight involves operations above 12,000 ft MSL
questions.why: 135.117(a)(7) says that if the flight involves operations above 12,000 feet MSL, the briefing covers the normal and emergency use of oxygen [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. The sentence names the altitude flown and never says cabin pressure altitude. Where the Part 135 oxygen rules mean the cabin, they say so: 135.89(b)(1) and 135.157(b) both use the words 'cabin pressure altitude' [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]] [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]. FL 230 is above 12,000 ft MSL, and a decompression would bring the cabin up to that altitude, so the briefing is needed. The 30-minute clock belongs to the pilot and passenger supply rules, not to the briefing.

questions.q: A friend with a new commercial certificate will fly an unpressurized turbocharged single to 17,500 ft, using oxygen. Does the 14 CFR 61.31(g) high-altitude training requirement apply to him?
options: No. It covers pressurized airplanes whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL, though the AC highly recommends the training for anyone flying above 10,000 ft
Yes, because he will fly above 12,500 ft
Yes, because any flight that needs supplemental oxygen requires the endorsements
No, and the AC's high-altitude training is not meant for piston airplanes at all
questions.why: 61.31(g) applies to a pressurized aircraft whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. AC 61-107B says the same, and highly recommends the training for all pilots who fly above 10,000 ft MSL [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. The last choice is wrong: the AC says its training is meant mainly for reciprocating engine and turboprop airplanes [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

questions.q: In your pressurized single the cabin altimeter has crept up to 16,000 ft. You are breathing fast, but your fingertip pulse oximeter still shows a normal reading. What is the best action?
options: Wait; a normal oximeter reading means your brain is getting enough oxygen
Breathe faster to keep the oximeter reading up
Put on your oxygen now and start down; do not wait for the oximeter to fall
Recheck the oximeter in five minutes and act only if it drops
questions.why: The FAA cautions against using a pulse oximeter as the only sign of hypoxia: waiting for the saturation to fall may let you become impaired first, and a fingertip reading may not show the oxygen your brain gets because hyperventilation cuts blood flow to the brain [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. If hypoxia is suspected, mask on, 100 percent oxygen, then descend [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The rule agrees: with the cabin above 14,000 ft, the required crew must use oxygen the entire time, and above 15,000 ft each occupant must be provided with it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Breathing faster is the hyperventilation the AC warns about.

questions.q: Two pilots fly a pressurized jet at FL 430. Both are at the controls, and each has a quick-donning mask that goes on with one hand within 5 seconds. What does 91.211(b) require about masks?
options: Neither pilot has to wear a mask, because both have quick-donning masks and both are at the controls
One pilot at the controls must wear and use a sealed mask, because the two-pilot exception stops at FL 410
Both pilots must wear sealed masks at all times above FL 350
A mask is needed only if one pilot leaves the controls
questions.why: Above FL 350 one pilot at the controls must wear and use a secured, sealed mask. The exception, two pilots at the controls each with a quick-donning mask, is allowed only at or below FL 410 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]]. FL 430 is above that, so the exception is gone. Both pilots in masks is more than the rule asks for, and the leave-the-controls rule in (b)(2) is an extra requirement on top, not the only trigger [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]].

questions.q: After a trip you clean a crew oxygen mask that has a built-in microphone. Which method matches the PHAK?
options: Rinse the whole mask, microphone included, under running water, then air dry
Wipe it with a petroleum-based cleaner so the rubber stays soft
Leave it alone; washing damages the mask seal
Wash it with mild soap and water, use a clean swab instead of running water around the microphone, disinfect it, then wipe and air dry
questions.why: The PHAK says to wash a mask with a mild soap and water solution, and if a microphone is installed to use a clean swab instead of running water to wipe off the soap; then disinfect it, wipe it with a clean cloth and air dry [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. A petroleum cleaner is the worst choice near oxygen: oils and greases may ignite in oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and oxygen under pressure reacts with petroleum products [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

questions.q: You will practice a simulated rapid decompression and emergency descent in your pressurized single on an IFR flight at FL 220. What does AC 61-107B say about the ATC side of it?
options: Coordinate with ATC in advance, and do not leave your assigned altitude without a clearance
Start down as soon as your mask is on, since ATC will see the descent on radar
Squawk 7700 so ATC clears the airspace below you
Skip the mask and oxygen controls, since nothing is really depressurized
questions.why: For training, the AC says to simulate the decompression by donning the masks, turning on the oxygen controls, configuring for and flying the emergency descent, to coordinate with ATC in advance, and not to vacate any assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. A descent started on your own breaks the clearance, and skipping the masks and oxygen controls leaves out the part you are there to practice. 61.31(g) flight training is likewise done without actually depressurizing [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

questions.q: After a decompression you will be on the mask and talking to ATC during the descent. Which step in the AFH preflight oxygen test makes sure you can?
options: Checking that the cabin altitude warning sounds
Measuring the flow at each passenger mask
Pilot and ATC communication using the mask microphones
Purging the regulator hose of air
questions.why: The AFH high-altitude training outline lists, in the oxygen functional test, pilot and ATC communication using mask microphones, along with supply and pressure, regulator operation, oxygen flow and mask fit [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]. AC 61-107B also says to demonstrate communications with ATC using the oxygen equipment [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12c]]. Crew masks usually contain a microphone [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. After a decompression the mask goes on first and stays on for the descent [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]], so a dead microphone would show up at the worst time. The other three checks are fine ideas, but none of them tests talking.

questions.q: Before a flight in your pressurized single, a passenger says he has a bad head cold and offers to use a decongestant nasal spray. A rapid descent after a pressure loss is always possible. What does the AIM say?
options: The spray is enough; the AIM says decongestant sprays and drops give adequate protection
A cold does not matter, because a pressurized cabin never changes pressure fast enough to hurt
An ear block happens only on the way up, so a descent is not a concern
An ear block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection; sprays and drops usually do not protect enough
questions.why: A cold or sore throat can make the ears hard to equalize, and the AIM says the pressure difference can hold the eustachian tube closed, especially during descent, causing severe ear pain and hearing loss that can last hours to days. It is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection, and decongestant sprays or drops usually do not give adequate protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. After a pressure loss you would be descending fast, which is the application that makes the cold matter in this airplane.

questions.q: You plan a flight over high terrain in your pressurized single. Your oxygen duration chart shows the bottle covers your planned time at altitude with nothing to spare. What does AC 61-107B advise?
options: When possible, carry additional oxygen for emergencies, since breathing rates rise under stress and extra could be needed
Nothing more, because duration charts already include a reserve for emergencies
Extra oxygen is advised only for flights above FL 250
Use the pulse oximeter to ration the oxygen so the bottle lasts longer
questions.why: In flight planning the AC lists oxygen duration charts, then says that when possible additional oxygen should be provided to allow for emergency situations, because breathing rates increase under stress and extra oxygen could be necessary [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-6a]] [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6a]]. The sources do not say duration charts include a reserve, and they set no FL 250 limit on the advice. After a pressure loss over high terrain you may have to stay high longer than planned.

questions.q: In the briefing for your pressurized single, a passenger in the window seat says he will loosen his belt after takeoff because the cabin is pressurized and the air is smooth. What do you tell him?
options: He may loosen it once the cabin altitude is below 8,000 ft, because structural damage cannot happen at a low cabin altitude
Belts matter only for takeoff and landing, as in an unpressurized airplane
Keep it fastened whenever he is seated, because if a window or door fails, people near an opening can be tossed or blown out
Only the pilot's belt matters, because the pressure hull protects the passengers
questions.why: Structural damage can toss or blow people out through an opening, so the PHAK says people near openings should wear safety harnesses or seat belts at all times while the airplane is pressurized and they are seated [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Loose items also move toward a large opening, so the AC adds that baggage and oxygen cylinders must be secured [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. A low cabin altitude says nothing about the strength of the window.

questions.q: Part 91, pressurized single at FL 280. The 10-minute descent supply for each occupant is all the oxygen you can count on after a decompression. Your descent over rough terrain averages only 1,500 fpm, and you want to reach 10,000 ft, the level AC 61-107B prefers. How long is the descent, and does the 10-minute supply cover it?
options: About 8.7 minutes, so the 10-minute supply covers it
About 12 minutes, so the supply runs out about 2 minutes before you reach 10,000 ft
About 18.7 minutes, so the supply covers little more than half of it
About 10.3 minutes, so the supply runs out about 20 seconds short
questions.why: (28,000 - 10,000) / 1,500 = 12.0 minutes. The AC's hypoxia drill says descend, preferably below 10,000 ft [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Above FL 250 the rule requires at least a 10-minute supply for each occupant, in addition to the oxygen paragraph (a) requires [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], so that 10 minutes is a minimum, and here it falls 2 minutes short of the way down. 8.7 minutes is the time to 15,000 ft only, 10.3 minutes is the time to 12,500 ft, and 18.7 minutes is the time from FL 280 to sea level.
